title: The State Is Enough
dek: A Markov process is a bet: that you can choose a description of "now" so complete that the past adds nothing. This is what that bet buys — matrices you can raise to a power, stationary distributions, mixing times — and where computer science has cashed it: PageRank, MCMC, Viterbi, Kalman, MDPs and reinforcement learning, branch predictors, cache models, queueing and capacity planning, and the state-size fight between attention and state-space models. It closes with where the bet loses.
byline: 28 September 2026 · Every number in a figure is computed from the model printed beside it
description: What a Markov process is, what the memoryless property buys you, and where computer science uses it: PageRank, MCMC, HMMs, MDPs, branch predictors, queueing, and modern sequence models.
og_description: The Markov property is a modelling bet, not a fact about the world: choose a state so complete that history adds nothing. This explainer works through the arithmetic — transition matrices, stationary distributions, spectral gaps, generators — and then through the places computer science cashes it: PageRank and random walks, Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs, Viterbi and Kalman, MDPs and RL, two-bit branch predictors, Markov prefetchers, M/M/1 queues and capacity planning, diffusion models, and the KV-cache-versus-recurrent-state argument in sequence architectures.
twitter_description: Markov processes, taken apart: the memoryless bet, the arithmetic it buys, and fourteen places computer science cashes it — from PageRank to branch predictors to the state-size fight between attention and SSMs.

sections.title: The memoryless bet
figures: fig-screen · conditioning diagram (SVG, wide) · a trajectory with a screen at t: the past is blocked, the present carries everything
fig-order-k · state augmentation (SVG) · an order-2 chain on {a,b} redrawn as a first-order chain on pairs
sections.brief: Definition first, informally then formally. P(X_{t+1} | X_t, ..., X_0) = P(X_{t+1} | X_t). The key move: memorylessness is a property of the pair (process, state space), not of the world. Any finite-order dependence becomes first-order by putting the history in the state. Markov 1906; the 1913 Eugene Onegin vowel/consonant count. Shannon 1948 §3. Time-homogeneity as a separate assumption people forget.

sections.title: Four kinds of chain
figures: fig-quadrants · 2x2 taxonomy (SVG, wide) · discrete/continuous time x discrete/continuous state, with the CS model living in each cell
sections.brief: DTMC, CTMC, discrete-time continuous-state (Kalman, Langevin, diffusion models), diffusion/SDE. Plus the two orthogonal extensions that get called Markov: Markov random fields (index set is a graph, not time) and Markov decision processes (an action enters the transition). Name where each lands in CS.

sections.title: The arithmetic it buys you
figures: fig-powers · chain + matrix + convergence (SVG, wide) · a 3-state chain, its P, and the rows of P^n converging
fig-spectral · mixing curves (SVG) · TV distance vs step for three chains with different second eigenvalues
fig-absorbing · absorbing chain + fundamental matrix (SVG) · expected steps to absorption for a retry ladder
sections.brief: Row-stochastic matrix, Chapman-Kolmogorov, n-step = P^n, distribution as row vector. Stationary distribution as left eigenvector; Perron-Frobenius; irreducible + aperiodic => unique limit. Reversibility and detailed balance. Spectral gap and mixing time. Absorbing chains, fundamental matrix N = (I-Q)^-1, expected time to absorption. All numbers computed.

sections.title: Continuous time, and the forced exponential
figures: fig-holding · CTMC decomposition (SVG, wide) · generator Q splits into exponential holding times plus an embedded jump chain
sections.brief: Memorylessness in continuous time forces exponential holding times - prove it in three lines. Generator Q, off-diagonals are rates, rows sum to zero. Kolmogorov forward equation, P(t) = e^{Qt}. Embedded jump chain. Uniformisation. The Poisson process as the simplest CTMC. Semi-Markov as the escape hatch.

sections.title: The state is a design choice
figures: fig-augment · augmentation ladder (SVG, wide) · four models of the same stream, state size and what each can express
sections.brief: The engineering section. Augment until Markov, then pay for it: state-space size is the bill. Sufficient statistics. Lumpability. Partial observability: POMDP and the belief state; DQN's four-frame stack as the cheapest possible fix. Variable-order models (context trees, PPM). When to stop augmenting.

sections.title: Walking a graph: PageRank and after
figures: fig-pagerank · web graph + teleport (SVG, wide) · dangling nodes, the damping fix, and the computed ranks of an 8-page graph
sections.brief: PageRank is a stationary distribution, and damping is an engineering fix for reducibility and periodicity, not a model of boredom. Power iteration cost. Personalised PageRank. Random-walk embeddings (DeepWalk, node2vec), Pixie, spectral clustering's conductance connection.

sections.title: Sampling by walking: MCMC
figures: fig-mh · Metropolis-Hastings loop + acceptance (SVG, wide) · the accept rule, why detailed balance holds, and measured acceptance vs step size
sections.brief: The inversion: design the chain so its stationary distribution is the target. Metropolis 1953, Hastings 1970, Gibbs. Detailed balance as a sufficient condition. Why the normalising constant cancels. Simulated annealing, HMC/NUTS, probabilistic programming. Diagnostics: burn-in, R-hat, effective sample size. Honest note: mixing time is the whole game and nobody can bound it in practice.

sections.title: Hidden state: Viterbi, Baum-Welch, Kalman
figures: fig-trellis · Viterbi trellis (SVG, wide) · a worked decode with computed log-probabilities on every surviving path
sections.brief: HMMs: the chain is hidden, you see emissions. Forward algorithm, Viterbi (1967) as dynamic programming over a trellis, Baum-Welch as EM. Where it was load-bearing: speech recognition until ~2012, POS tagging, gene finding, keyboard decoding, and Viterbi decoding in convolutional codes. Kalman filter (1960) as the continuous-state Gaussian case; sensor fusion, SLAM, GPS. One worked trellis with real numbers.

sections.title: Decisions: MDPs and reinforcement learning
figures: fig-mdp · the loop and the backup (SVG, wide) · agent-environment loop on the left, the Bellman backup tree on the right
fig-value-iteration · computed convergence (SVG) · value iteration on a small gridworld, values per sweep
sections.brief: Bellman 1957, Howard 1960. (S,A,P,R,gamma). Bellman optimality, value and policy iteration, contraction with modulus gamma. Model-free: TD, Q-learning, policy gradient. Bandits as one-state MDPs. Production uses: AlphaGo/MuZero, datacentre cooling, chip floorplanning, compiler heuristics (MLGO), congestion control, and RLHF - with the honest note that RLHF's 'MDP' is mostly a one-step or token-level bandit.

sections.title: Chains inside the machine
figures: fig-2bit · saturating counter as a chain (SVG, wide) · the four-state predictor, its transition matrix, and computed misprediction rate vs taken-rate
fig-prefetch · Markov prefetcher table (HTML table) · address-to-successor table, the state, and what it costs
sections.brief: The architecture section. Smith's 2-bit saturating counter is literally a 4-state Markov chain - derive the misprediction rate. Higher-order predictors (gshare, TAGE) are state augmentation in silicon. Markov prefetchers (Joseph & Grunwald 1997). Cache replacement as a chain; the Che approximation and why LRU hit rate is analytically awkward. Randomised algorithms: Schoening's random walk for 3-SAT, skip lists, gossip/epidemic protocols, load balancing.

sections.title: Queues, capacity, and failure
figures: fig-mm1 · birth-death chain + the utilisation wall (SVG, wide) · M/M/1 states, the rho/(1-rho) curve, and a computed capacity table
fig-availability · two-state CTMC (SVG) · up/down with MTTF and MTTR, and the nines it implies
sections.brief: Erlang, Kendall notation, Little's law. M/M/1 as a birth-death CTMC; queue length rho/(1-rho); why latency explodes past 70% utilisation - computed table. M/M/c and Erlang-C for thread pools and call centres. Two-state availability CTMC and the nines. Then the warning that section 14 collects: real arrivals are not Poisson.

sections.title: Sequence models and the size of the state
figures: fig-state-size · state-size axis (SVG, wide) · n-gram, RNN, SSM, sliding window, full attention - bytes of state vs what it can express, with a computed KV-cache size
fig-diffusion · forward and reverse chain (SVG) · the fixed noising chain and the learned reverse
sections.brief: Shannon's n-grams were Markov models of English. Autoregressive decoding is a Markov process on whatever you carry forward: an RNN/SSM carries a fixed-size state (Markov, bounded), attention carries a KV cache that grows with t (still Markov, but on a state that grows) - compute the bytes for a concrete model. This is exactly the architectural argument of 2023-2026: S4, Mamba, RWKV, linear attention, sliding windows, hybrid stacks. Diffusion models as Markov chains. Speculative decoding needs the chain's memorylessness to be exactly right.

sections.title: Agent loops as processes
figures: fig-agent · the agent loop as an MDP (SVG, wide) · context as state, tool calls as actions, verification as terminal reward
sections.brief: My own framing, badged as such. An agent session looks like an MDP: context is the state, tool calls are actions, and the environment is a filesystem plus a set of services. But the state is not the context window - it is the environment, and the context is a lossy observation of it, which makes the honest model a POMDP. Connects to the quirq programme: budget B, snapshots S0/S1, verified score V as a terminal reward, cost C_total as the discount you actually pay. What this buys: episodes become comparable; what it does not buy: the transition kernel is unknown and non-stationary.

sections.title: Where the bet loses
figures: fig-tails · exponential vs heavy tail (SVG, wide) · the same mean, two tails, and the computed P(X > 10x mean)
sections.brief: The honest-limits section. Heavy tails and self-similarity: Leland et al. 1994 showed Ethernet traffic is not Poisson, and the same holds for web and datacentre traffic - what that breaks in M/M/1 reasoning. Non-stationarity. State explosion and the curse of dimensionality. Partial observability. Unknown mixing time. Model mismatch in RL. The rule of thumb: use Markov models for structure and bounds, not for predictions you would bet a pager on.
